newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's Buyoya to investigate alleged massacres.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya to investigate alleged massacres.

text.p: Burundi's military leader Major Pierre Buyoya on Thursday promised to investigate reports by the United Nations that his mainly Tutsi army has killed at least 1,000 people since the start of December.
Buyoya, in power since the army staged a coup last year, told U.N. officials at a meeting in Bujumbura that he would take action against whoever was found to have been responsible for the killings.
"We shall investigate these reports and see whether there is any truth in them. If true, those found involved will be punished," said a statement issued by Buyoya's office after the meeting.

But Buyoya also reminded the U.N. officials that many people were being killed in crossfire in a brutal war between his army and rebels of the Hutu majority fighting for a greater political stake in the tiny central African nation.

Buyoya's reaction came a day after the U.N. human rights office, issuing evidence of the killings in the seven weeks to January 21, said they marked a new escalation in violence in Burundi's three-year guerrilla war.
In a statement, it said Hutu rebels who are also accused of massacres of civilians in the increasingly dirty war were responsible for the killing of 58 people in the same period.
Worsening violence was accompanied by an army policy of forceful relocation of Hutu peasants and increasing use of mines by the warring sides, the Geneva-based U.N. body said.
The latest killings come on top of army massacres of more than 1,100 majority Hutus in October and November in the tiny central African country, according to human rights observers.
"The human rights situation in Burundi was characterised by a new and more serious outburst of violence and military operations in the reporting period," the U.N. statement said.

The army routinely denies killing Hutus and blames rebels for the massacres. Tutsis are outnumbered four-to-one in Burundi and many fear they will perish unless they retain full control of the army and block real power-sharing with Hutus.

U.N. human rights observers said they were having increasing difficulty in investigating massacres because of worsening insecurity, which has made large swathes of the mountainous country no-go areas for foreign relief workers.

More than 150,000 people have been killed in war between the army and Hutu rebels and massacres since October 1993 when Burundi's first elected Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, was murdered by renegade Tutsi soldiers.
Regional states imposed a transport and economic blockade on Burundi one week after Buyoya's coup in July in an attempt to force a return to civilian rule.
